procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench dated April 5, 1963 in Criminal Misc. Case No. 135 of 1962, which directed that the 21 currency notes be handed over to the first and second respondents.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The appellant (bank) applied to the Fourth Additional Sessions Judge, Indore under section 517(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the return of the currency notes, which was allowed on April 24, 1962.
2. The State of Madhya Pradesh filed an appeal to the High Court, which allowed the appeal, set aside the trial court's order of acquittal of the third respondent, and convicted him.
3. The first respondent applied to the High Court for delivery of the currency notes to him and the second respondent.
4. The High Court, by its order dated April 5, 1963, allowed the application and directed that the notes be handed over to the first and second respondents.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (bank) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, contending that the High Court reversed the Sessions Judge's order without giving notice or an opportunity to be heard, violating principles of natural justice. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the currency notes to be returned to the appellant.

directions: set aside the order of the High Court dated April 5, 1963
direct that the 21 currency notes of the denomination of Rs. 1000 each seized by the Madhya Pradesh Police should be returned to the appellant

issue.issue_text: Whether it is necessary to give a party adversely affected a notice of hearing and an opportunity to be heard before an order for the return of seized property under Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is passed.

facts: The High Court reversed a trial court's order that had directed seized currency notes to be returned to the appellant.
The High Court made this decision without giving the appellant any notice or an opportunity to be heard.
The appellant argued that this violated the principles of natural justice.
The respondents countered that the relevant sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure (517 and 520) do not explicitly require notice to be given.
law: The Court acknowledged that the statute (Code of Criminal Procedure) is silent and does not expressly require that notice be issued or a hearing be given to adversely affected parties.
However, the Court invoked a fundamental principle of natural justice: "no man is to be deprived of his property without his having an opportunity of being heard."
This principle, established in the case of *Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works*, is considered a "necessary implication" in the law, even when a statute does not explicitly state it.
The Court described this rule as being of "universal application and founded upon the plainest principles of justice."
application: The Court applied this principle of natural justice directly to the case.

It reasoned that even though the statute was silent, the High Court was still bound to hear the appellant before making an order that would adversely affect them (i.e., deprive them of the property they were set to receive).
By reversing the trial court's order without giving the appellant notice, the High Court deprived the appellant of property without a hearing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there is a necessary legal implication that a party who will be adversely affected by an order for the return of seized property must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard. Because the High Court failed to do this, its order was "vitiated in law" and illegal.

issue.issue_text: Who has the 'right to possess' seized currency notes within the meaning of Section 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an innocent party who received them in the normal course of business, or the original owners who parted with them for a criminal purpose.

facts: The appellant bank received currency notes in the normal course of its business, acting in good faith and without any knowledge that the notes were involved in a crime.
The original owners (respondents 1 and 2) had voluntarily handed over these same currency notes to a third party for the "criminal purpose of duplication."
The police seized the notes from the appellant bank as part of a criminal investigation against the third party.
law: Section 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure grants a court the discretion to order the delivery of seized property to any person "claiming to be entitled to possession thereof."

The Court cited the legal principle that property in currency notes passes by mere delivery. This is a well-established exception to the general rule that a person cannot transfer a better title than they themselves have (*Nemo dat quod non habet*).

This exception for currency is based on commercial necessity and applies only if the recipient takes the notes in good faith, for value, and without notice of any defect in the previous owner's title.
application: The Court first determined that the two parties were not equally innocent. The original owners had parted with their money for a criminal purpose, which weakened their claim.

In contrast, the appellant bank met all the conditions for the legal exception regarding currency. It had received the notes in good faith, for value, and in the normal course of business, with no suspicion of wrongdoing.
Because property in currency passes by delivery to a good-faith recipient, the bank had acquired a valid right to possess the notes.
The Court reasoned that the bank's innocent acquisition in the course of business gave it a superior claim to possession over the original owners who had used the notes for an illegal purpose.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellant bank, as the innocent party who received the currency notes in the normal course of business, had the 'right to possess' them under Section 517. The original owners' claim was weaker because they had parted with the notes for a criminal purpose.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its discretion under Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order the return of currency notes to the original owners.

facts: The appellant bank received 21 currency notes in the normal course of its business.
The respondents (original owners) had handed over these notes to a third party for the 'criminal purpose of duplication'.
The appellant bank acted in good faith, without any knowledge or suspicion that the notes were involved in a crime.
The respondents did not allege any fraud or lack of good faith on the part of the appellant bank.
law: Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure grant the High Court discretion in disposing of property related to a crime.
This discretion must be exercised according to proper legal principles.
A key legal principle is that property in currency notes passes by mere delivery, which is an exception to the rule 'Nemo dat quod non habet' (no one can give what they do not have).
This exception applies if the transferee (the person receiving the notes) takes them in good faith, for value, and without notice of any defect in the transferor's title.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not exercised its discretion according to the correct legal principles.
The Court applied the principle that property in currency passes by delivery to a bona fide transferee for value.
The appellant bank met these conditions: it received the notes in the normal course of business (for value) and in good faith, without knowledge of the crime.
In contrast, the respondents were not equally innocent, as they had handed over the notes for a criminal purpose.
Therefore, the appellant bank had acquired a valid 'right to possess' the currency notes under Section 517 of the Code.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in ordering the return of the currency notes to the original owners (respondents). The High Court erred by not applying the correct legal principles regarding the transfer of currency. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed that the notes be returned to the appellant bank.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is necessary to give a party adversely affected a notice of hearing and an opportunity to be heard before an order for the return of seized property under Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is passed.
appellant_arguments: The High Court reversed the trial court's order without giving the appellant notice or an opportunity to be heard.
The High Court's order was a violation of the principles of natural justice and was therefore illegal.
respondent_arguments: There is no provision in Section 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that requires giving notice to affected parties.
The High Court's order cannot be challenged on the ground that no hearing was given to the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Who has the 'right to possess' seized currency notes within the meaning of Section 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an innocent party who received them in the normal course of business, or the original owners who parted with them for a criminal purpose.
appellant_arguments: The appellant obtained the currency notes in the normal course of its business without any knowledge or suspicion of them being involved in an offence.
Property in currency notes passes by mere delivery, giving the appellant the 'right to possess' them under Section 517.
The respondents are not equally innocent because they handed over the currency notes for the 'criminal purpose of duplication'.
respondent_arguments: The currency notes belonged to the respondents, and they were deprived of them by the commission of an offence.
The issue is about which of two innocent parties should suffer: the one who lost the property due to a criminal act, or the one who received it in the course of business.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its discretion under Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to order the return of currency notes to the original owners.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's discretion was not exercised according to proper legal principle, as the respondents were not innocent parties, having parted with the notes for a criminal purpose.
respondent_arguments: The High Court has discretion under the statute to decide to whom the property should be returned.
The Supreme Court should not interfere with the High Court's exercise of its discretion.

cases.case_name: Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works
cases.principle: Even if a statute is silent and does not expressly require a notice to be issued or a hearing to be given, there is a necessary implication in law that a party adversely affected should be heard before being deprived of their property.
To reaffirm the principle that although there are no positive words in a statute requiring that a party shall be heard, the justice of the common law will supply the omission of the legislature.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order reversing a lower court's decision on the disposal of property is legally invalid if made without giving notice and an opportunity to be heard to the adversely affected party, as the principles of natural justice require a hearing even if the statute is silent. Substantively, property in currency notes passes by mere delivery to a transferee who acquires them in good faith for value and without notice of any defect in the transferor's title.
obiter: The court does not express any concluded opinion on the ultimate question of liability for payment of the money as between the parties.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred both procedurally and on the merits. Procedurally, its order was vitiated in law because it violated the principles of natural justice by failing to give the appellant notice and an opportunity to be heard before reversing an order in its favor. On the merits, the High Court improperly exercised its discretion by ordering the return of currency notes to the respondents, who were not innocent parties because they had parted with the notes for a criminal purpose, whereas the appellant, having received the notes in good faith during the normal course of business, had a superior right to possession under the legal principle that property in currency passes by delivery.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem): 'though the statute is silent and does not expressly require issue of any notice there is in the eye of law a necessary implication that the party adversely affected should be heard bfore the Court makes an order for return oi the seized property.'

The rule of transfer of property in currency: 'property in coins and currency notes passes by mere delivery and it is the clearest exception to the rule N emo dat quod non habat... But the exception only applies if the transferee of the coin. or currency notes takes in good faith for value and without notice of a defect in the title of the transforor.'

The standard for judicial discretion: Discretion conferred by statute, such as under Sections 517 and 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, must be exercised 'according to proper legal orinciole' and an order failing this standard is 'liable to be set aside.'
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's argument that Section 520 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not require notice was rejected because 'although there are no positive words in a statute requiring that the party shall be heard, yet the justice of the common law will supply the omission of the legislature.'

The respondent's claim to be an equally innocent party was rejected by the court, which found 'it is.not, however, correct to say that respondents 1 and 2 are equa 11 y innocent because respondents 1 and 2 had admittedly handed over the currency notes to respondent No. 3 "for the criminal purpose of duplication".'

The respondent's argument that the Supreme Court should not interfere with the High Court's discretion was dismissed because 'the High Court has not exercised its discretion according to proper legal orinciole and its order is hence liable to be set aside.'
why_respondent_won: The appellant's position that the High Court's order was illegal for lack of notice was accepted, as the court held 'it is manifest that the High Court was bound to give notice to the appellant before reversing the order... As no such notice was given to the appellant, the order of the High Court dated 5th April, 1963 is vitiated in law.'

The appellant successfully established its 'right to possess' the currency notes because it 'obtained the currency notes in the normal course of its business and without any knowledge or suspicion,' and under the law, 'property in the currency notes, passed in its favour by mere delivery.'
policy_considerations: The rule that property in currency passes by delivery 'was engrafted in the interest of commercial necessity.'
The principle of natural justice requiring a hearing before a person is deprived of property is 'of universal application and founded upon the plainest principles of justice.'
